battle.title: Blueprint Under Pressure
battle.description: Walk through a system design round in a clear order the interviewer can follow.

questions.text: The interviewer says: "Design a URL shortener." What do you do FIRST?
options: Draw boxes for load balancers, caches and shards immediately
Pick a database and start writing the schema
Clarify requirements: features, expected scale, read/write ratio, and availability needs
Describe how Bitly works from memory
questions.answer: Clarify requirements: features, expected scale, read/write ratio, and availability needs
questions.explanation: Requirements and scale drive every later choice, so they come first. Drawing boxes or picking a database early commits you to a design before you know the problem.

questions.text: Which order is the most sensible way to structure a design round?
options: Requirements, rough capacity estimates, high-level design, deep dive on key parts, bottlenecks and trade-offs
Deep dive on one component, then requirements, then a diagram
Database schema, then code, then requirements
Technology list, then scale, then a summary
questions.answer: Requirements, rough capacity estimates, high-level design, deep dive on key parts, bottlenecks and trade-offs
questions.explanation: Going from broad to narrow keeps the interviewer oriented and gives you room to adjust. Starting deep or with technologies makes the answer hard to follow and easy to derail.

questions.text: Ten minutes in, the interviewer says nothing and you are unsure whether to continue. What is the best habit?
options: Keep talking faster so there is no silence
Stop and wait for the interviewer to guide every step
Pause, summarise the design so far, and ask which area they would like to explore deeper
Switch to a completely different design to look flexible
questions.answer: Pause, summarise the design so far, and ask which area they would like to explore deeper
questions.explanation: A design round is a collaboration, so check in and let the interviewer steer you to the area they care about. Rushing or waiting passively ignores that, and restarting wastes the progress you made.

questions.text: You propose a single database and the interviewer asks what happens at 100x traffic. What is the strongest reply?
options: That will never happen, so it is fine
Find the bottleneck first, then add caching, replicas or sharding as needed, noting each cost
I would switch to a more expensive server and call it done
We will use microservices, which fixes all scaling problems
questions.answer: Find the bottleneck first, then add caching, replicas or sharding as needed, noting each cost
questions.explanation: Scaling answers should be driven by the actual bottleneck and include the cost of each step, such as cache invalidation or replication lag. Buzzwords like 'microservices fix everything' show no reasoning.

questions.text: You realise midway that your design has a flaw in how it handles failures. What do you do?
options: Hope the interviewer does not notice and carry on
Point it out, explain the failure scenario, and show a fix such as retries or replication
Blame the vague requirements
Restart the whole design from scratch in silence
questions.answer: Point it out, explain the failure scenario, and show a fix such as retries or replication
questions.explanation: Spotting and fixing your own flaw is a strong signal of engineering maturity. Hiding it is risky and dishonest, and blaming requirements or silently restarting shows poor ownership.
